items.title: Neoclouds sell off: CoreWeave falls 10% to a 52-week low as Nebius takes a one-year, $3.5B loan from Citi
items.summary: Nebius's 364-day secured loan from Citi costs SOFR + 2.75% and will fund data centers and GPUs. Nebius says it still has over $40B of investment-grade contracts it can borrow against. CoreWeave closed at $55.60 after Bernstein cut its target to $51, estimating CoreWeave needs about $85B to fund its committed backlog, and some CoreWeave bonds now yield around 15%, up from 9.675% when they were issued (per Motley Fool and press reports).
items.why: The GPU build-out runs on borrowed money, so the cost of that debt is now a real limit on how fast neoclouds can add capacity, whatever Jensen Huang says about demand being "off the charts."
items.body:
Marks next step in Nebius’s strategy to fund global capacity build-out on attractive terms
Advances diversified capital structure built on a disciplined balance sheet
Increases flexibility over timing and structure of longer-term financing to fuel growth in 2027 and beyond
Amsterdam, 22 October, 2026 — Nebius Group N.V. (Nasdaq: NBIS), the AI cloud company, today announced that it has entered into a $3.5 billion senior secured facility provided by Citi.
The facility provides access to capital at attractive rates to support Nebius’s global capacity build-out, and advances the company’s diversified and sequenced funding strategy.
It complements a funding base that includes customer prepayments and operating cash flows with other financing mechanisms.
This provides flexibility over the timing and structure of further external capital-raising as the company continues to execute on its global build-out plans.
Ophir Nave, Chief Operating Officer of Nebius, said:
“We continue to execute our funding strategy as planned, and are pleased to have secured this financing from a leading global financial institution. This is a result of our disciplined approach to managing our balance sheet to fund our portfolio of projects, and once again demonstrates our ability to choose when and how we raise capital to support our growth.
“Sequencing our financing is how we optimize our long-term cost of capital. This facility provides additional financing to support our near-term capacity build-out. We still have a range of capital sources available to us to finance the next phase of growth, including asset-backed financing based on investment-grade customer commitments of more than $40 billion of long-term contracts.”
The facility has a 364-day maturity and initially bears interest at Term SOFR plus 2.75% per annum, increasing up to a maximum of 3.50% per annum, and subject to other adjustments.
The proceeds will be used for data center development and GPU procurement, as well as for general corporate purposes.
Citi acted as mandated lead arranger, agent and security agent.
Nebius, the AI cloud company, is building the full-stack platform for developers and companies to take charge of their AI future — from data and model training to production deployment. Founded on deep in-house technological expertise and operating at scale with a rapidly expanding global footprint, Nebius serves startups and enterprises building AI products, agents, and services worldwide. Nebius is listed on Nasdaq (Nasdaq: NBIS) and headquartered in Amsterdam.
For more information please visit nebius.com
Media relations: media@nebius.com Investor relations: askIR@nebius.com

items.title: Meta spent $34.9B on capex last quarter, and its free cash flow went negative
items.summary: Revenue rose 26% to $64.6B, but free cash flow was −$2.1B, down from $10.6B a year ago. Meta narrowed its 2026 capex guidance to $135–145B. Zuckerberg said more than 10M people in the US and Canada have set up the Muse assistant, that it isn't global yet because it needs so much compute, and that "it's going to be very important to get the math on all of this to work out."
items.why: A hyperscaler whose capex now exceeds its operating cash flow is one more reason AI infrastructure is moving to debt financing, the same pressure showing up in neocloud credit.
items.body:
Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta Platforms topped Wall Street revenue targets in the third quarter and forecast continued top-line growth, even as billions in legal payments for teen mental health litigation cut its operating margins in half, and massive AI investments pushed free cash flow into negative territory.
The company also said it create a Class C stock share class to help it fund the AI buildout, pay employee stock compensation, and fund acquisitions.
Investors ignored the short-term pain for the potential of a future AI payoff, cheering early signs of traction with the recently released Muse AI agent, sending Meta shares up as much as 5% in after-hours trading on Wednesday.
“Our investments are paying off, the core business is strong, and we’re seeing velocity across the board,” Zuckerberg said in a prepared statement on Wednesday, later adding on the conference call that plans were underway to monetize Muse.
“The average revenue per American user for our existing ‘family of apps’ users is several hundreds of dollars annually, and we expect Muse will reach an even higher level over time due to the amount of commerce that we already see taking place,” Zuckerberg said.
Meta’s third-quarter revenue rose 26% to $64.6 billion, above the $63.3 billion analysts expected, according to Visible Alpha consensus from S&P Global Market Intelligence. And the company forecast revenue for the final quarter of the year to range between $73 billion and $76 billion, compared with the $73.75 billion expected by analysts.
But Meta’s operating income of $13 billion was down 37% from the $20.5 billion it posted in the second quarter of 2025 as a result of a $10 billion settlement Meta struck with a group of attorneys general over youth safety. The terms of the settlement will see Meta pay about $18 billion to the states over the next decade, depending on cooperation from TikTok and Google’s YouTube. Without the charge, operating income would have been $22.9 billion and earnings of $7.40 a share, rather than $13 billion and $3.83.
Legal issues may continue to take a bite out of Meta’s results. Hours before Meta announced its Q3 results Wednesday, news broke that a New Mexico judge had ordered the company to pay $25 billion in penalties related to the Cambridge Analytica data privacy scandal. Meta plans to appeal.
Net income in Q3 totaled $9.9 billion, or $3.83 a share, versus $2.7 billion, or $1.05 a share in the year-ago period.
Meta is plowing unprecedented amounts of capital into AI infrastructure and services, joining companies like Alphabet , OpenAI, and Microsoft in a race to develop the most advanced AI models. To continue funding the AI effort, Meta said it would reallocate investments from its money-losing virtual reality business, Reality Labs, and that it would create a new nonvoting class C common stock.
Capital expenditures, which have tech investors on tenterhooks, clocked in at $34.9 billion, compared with $31 billion in the second quarter and $19.4 billion a year ago. Meta slightly tweaked its full year capex guidance to $135 billion to $145 billion, from $130 billion to $145 billion.
Free cash flow, which has been a sore spot for Meta, was negative $2.1 billion, compared with $784 million in the second quarter and $10.6 billion a year ago.
The results also come a week after Meta’s Superintelligence Labs launched Muse Wonder to the public, its first frontier model , and a little over a month since Meta released its Muse virtual assistant.

So Nebius will need longer-term money behind it soon. It says it has over $40B of investment-grade contracts to borrow against, which is how it gets to pick its timing.

Then Meta. $34.9B of capex last quarter, free cash flow of negative $2.1B versus $10.6B a year ago, and a new nonvoting Class C stock to help fund the buildout.

We talk about GPU supply and power. This week the number setting the pace looks like the interest rate.
